# Horizon-free bounded-bit marking on uniform rational metrics

Problem: TOP-30007490  
Claim type: Partial result  
Author: /root/hundred_algorithms

**Exact scope.** For every finite uniform rational metric of distance Δ>0 and 2≤k<n, a single randomized bit algorithm uses polynomial preprocessing and worst-case polynomial work per request in L+log(t+1), and has expected cost≤2Hk·OPT+2kΔ for every finite oblivious sequence from a common initial k-point configuration. This satisfies the prompt on uniform metrics, not arbitrary finite metrics.

The classical marking algorithm is 2Hk-competitive on uniform metrics [1, Theorem1]. Its usual instruction to choose a uniform victim does not by itself establish a strict worst-case per-request fair-bit time bound: rejection sampling may take arbitrarily many trials. We give a finite-bit implementation and bound its entire horizon-free error through the phase structure.

Partition requests into maximal consecutive phases containing at most k distinct points. Mark points when requested in the current phase; on the first request that would exceed k marks, clear the marks and begin the next phase. A hit marks its point. On a miss choose an unmarked cached point, evict it, move that server to the requested point, and mark the request. A miss always has an available victim. Every phase has at most k misses, and at the end of a complete phase the cache is exactly its k distinct requested points, independently of random choices.

First consider ideal uniform victim choice. In a phase after the first, let ℓ be the number of clean points not in the preceding phase. Clean requests each fault once. For the j-th previously unrequested old point, symmetry among the k−j+1 old points not requested earlier in this phase bounds its fault probability by ℓ/(k−j+1): at most ℓ of them are absent due to clean arrivals. Subsequent requests to a marked point cannot fault. Summing over the k−ℓ old points gives expected phase faults at most ℓ(1+Hk−Hℓ)≤ℓHk. This is the classical marking phase argument, not a new competitive ratio.

The union of two successive complete phases has k+ℓ distinct requested points. Any k-cache offline strategy must incur at least ℓ faults over that pair, irrespective of its initial cache. Summing these overlapping pairs counts every offline fault at most twice. The first phase contributes at most k algorithm faults. The same argument applies to a final partial phase by extending it for analysis or directly using its no-larger old-point sum. Thus ideal expected faults≤2Hk·OPT_faults+k.

For a deterministic time bound, at request number t≥1 and with q≤k eligible victims, use b=⌈log₂(8k(t+1)²)⌉ independent fair bits, interpret their value as U∈{0,…,2ᵇ−1}, and choose victim index floor(qU/2ᵇ). Each victim probability differs from 1/q by at most 2^(−b). Total variation distance from uniform is therefore at most q/2ᵇ≤δt=1/(8(t+1)²). There is no rejection loop, and all integer operands have O(log(k+1)+log(t+1)) bits.

Couple this algorithm to ideal marking separately within each phase. Their caches agree at each phase start, since the preceding completed phase forces the same cache. Until their first different victim, use a maximal coupling; its probability of differing during that phase is at most Σt∈phase δt. On any realized phase both algorithms fault at most k times, so the absolute phase cost difference is at most k. Consequently the expected excess over ideal marking, summed over any finite horizon, is at most
\[
 k\sum_{t\ge1}\delta_t<k/8.
\]
The same estimate covers the last partial phase. Multiplying by Δ and rounding the additive allowance upward gives expected cost≤2Hk·OPT+2kΔ. No horizon is known or estimated.

Maintain the cache and marks explicitly. Scanning at most n point identifiers and performing the bounded-bit calculation gives worst-case polynomial work in the metric’s full input length L plus log(t+1), for every random bit string. Checking that all off-diagonal rational distances equal Δ is polynomial preprocessing. The algorithm needs no numerical approximation to Δ: it only chooses which server to move. Since Hk≤1+ln k, this O(log k) ratio is also at most C log²(k+1) for a universal constant, covering the literal target on this metric subclass.

The proof uses oblivious requests: clean/stale identities and phase boundaries are fixed independently of random choices. It makes no arbitrary-metric embedding, no assertion about an adaptive adversary, and no validation of the separate2026 general-metric manuscript summarized by the earlier contribution.
